questions.question: The nucleus of every element after hydrogen holds two or more protons, packed tightly together. Like charges push each other away, and at that tiny distance the electric push between two protons is enormous. The strong nuclear force, the strongest of the four fundamental forces, holds the nucleus together all the same. How far does its pull reach from each proton or neutron?
questions.answer: To the particles right next to it
choices: To the particles right next to it
To every particle in the atom, electrons too
To the nuclei of the atoms around it
Across space, as far as gravity reaches
questions.context: The strong force pulls on protons and neutrons alike, about a hundred times harder than the electric push between two protons that close, but it fades to almost nothing beyond about two and a half trillionths of a millimetre, so each particle grips only its nearest neighbours and never reaches the next atom; electrons do not feel it at all. That is why a big nucleus such as uranium's is fragile: every proton pushes on every other proton, but grips only those beside it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science names the four fundamental forces and teaches that the strong force holds the nucleus together over a very short range.

questions.question: Between two protons, the pull of gravity is about a trillion trillion trillion times weaker than their electric push, and of the four fundamental forces, gravity is by far the weakest. Yet it is gravity, not the electric force, that holds the Moon on its path round Earth and Earth on its path round the Sun. Why does the weakest force win at that scale?
questions.answer: Mass only attracts, but plus and minus charges cancel out
choices: Mass only attracts, but plus and minus charges cancel out
The electric force fades with distance far faster than gravity
The electric force cannot travel across empty space
The Moon and Earth hold no charged particles at all
questions.context: Gravity only ever pulls, so the pull of every atom in Earth and the Moon adds up, while each holds almost exactly as much negative charge as positive, so its electric pushes and pulls cancel. Both forces fade with distance in the same way, and both reach across space without end. The other two forces, the strong force and the weak force behind some radioactive decay, reach no farther than a nucleus.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders compare the four fundamental forces, and charges cancelling while mass always adds up is the standard reason gravity rules the heavens.

questions.question: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann fired neutrons at uranium in Berlin late in 1938, and their careful chemical tests kept finding barium among the products. Hahn wrote for help to Lise Meitner, his research partner of some thirty years, who had fled Nazi Germany that summer. At Christmas in Sweden, she and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out what the barium meant. What had happened to the uranium?
questions.answer: Its nucleus had split into two smaller nuclei
choices: Its nucleus had split into two smaller nuclei
A neutron had chipped a small piece off its nucleus
Neutrons had built it up into a heavier element
The barium had been mixed in with it from the start
questions.context: Barium's nucleus holds 56 protons, little more than half of uranium's 92, so the uranium had not been chipped or built up: its nucleus had split into two middle-sized ones. Enrico Fermi and the Berlin team had earlier read such products as new elements heavier than uranium, and Hahn and Strassmann reported the barium but held back from explaining it; Frisch named the split fission, after the way a living cell divides. Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery, and Meitner was left out.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science tells the discovery of fission, and reading Hahn's barium as a split nucleus is the step Meitner and Frisch took.

questions.question: A helium nucleus is built of two protons and two neutrons. Measured with great care, it has a little less mass than two protons and two neutrons measured one by one, and the same shortfall turns up in every nucleus made of more than one particle. Physicists call it the mass defect. Why does a nucleus have less mass than its parts?
questions.answer: Some of their mass left as energy when they joined
choices: Some of their mass left as energy when they joined
Some of their mass is stored inside it as heat
Packed tightly, the particles take up less room
Gravity pulls more weakly on particles packed tight
questions.context: Albert Einstein's E = mc² says that mass and energy can turn into each other, and that a tiny mass is worth an enormous energy: one gram is worth about 90 trillion joules. When protons and neutrons bind into a nucleus, energy leaves and carries that sliver of mass away, so pulling the nucleus apart means putting the energy back; squeezing changes volume, not mass, and gravity changes weight, not mass. Chemical reactions shift mass too, but by about a billionth, far too little for any balance, which is why chemists find mass conserved.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches mass-energy equivalence, and the mass defect of a nucleus is the standard evidence that a little mass becomes a great deal of energy.

questions.question: Otto Frisch set out in Copenhagen in January 1939 to test the idea, his and Lise Meitner's, that a neutron can split a uranium nucleus in two. He lined a counting chamber with uranium, set a neutron source beside it, and made the counter record only pulses far bigger than uranium's own alpha particles could cause. Big pulses came. Which result would have counted most against the idea?
questions.answer: Big pulses still coming with the neutron source taken away
choices: Big pulses still coming with the neutron source taken away
No big pulses at all once the uranium lining was taken out
Twice as many big pulses with paraffin wax round the source
Fewer big pulses whenever a weaker neutron source was used
questions.context: No neutrons, no splitting: big pulses without the source would have meant something else was making them, but in hours of check runs Frisch saw none, and none without the uranium either. The count rose and fell with the strength of the source, and paraffin wax, which slows neutrons, doubled it, since slow neutrons split uranium more readily. Frisch called his pulses conclusive evidence that uranium nuclei were breaking into pieces of comparable size.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks which result would disprove a claim, and Frisch's check runs are a clean case of a test that could have failed.

questions.question: A uranium-235 nucleus can split in two, its pieces flying apart with great energy. In a reactor's fuel, one split can set off another, and that one another, in what physicists call a chain reaction. What carries the splitting from one nucleus to the next?
questions.answer: New neutrons thrown out by each split
choices: New neutrons thrown out by each split
Heat from each split, bursting the next nucleus
The two flying pieces of each split
Radiation from each split, weakening the next
questions.context: A uranium-235 nucleus splits when it captures a neutron, and each split throws out two or three new neutrons, which other uranium-235 nuclei can capture in turn. The two pieces carry most of the energy as speed, which turns to heat as they slow among the atoms around them, but they split nothing. A fuel pellet about a centimetre across gives about as much energy as a ton of coal, because a split frees millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction does.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science models the chain reaction, in which each fission frees neutrons that cause more fissions.

questions.question: In a nuclear power plant, splitting uranium heats water into steam, and the steam spins a turbine that drives a generator. Operators set how fast the uranium splits by sliding control rods, made of materials such as boron or cadmium, in and out of the reactor's core. Dropped all the way in, the rods stop the chain reaction. How do they do it?
questions.answer: They soak up neutrons before those split more nuclei
choices: They soak up neutrons before those split more nuclei
They slow the neutrons down so that fewer nuclei split
They cool the uranium until it stops splitting
They bounce the neutrons back out of the fuel
questions.context: Boron and cadmium capture neutrons, and every neutron a rod soaks up is one that cannot split another uranium nucleus, so pushing the rods in slows the reaction and pulling them out speeds it up. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, usually the water round the fuel, and slow neutrons split uranium-235 more readily, not less; the same water carries the heat away to make the steam.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn how a reactor controls fission, and control rods that absorb neutrons are the standard mechanism.

questions.question: Fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones. Fusion machines on Earth try to join deuterium and tritium, two heavy kinds of hydrogen, into helium, and they must first heat the fuel to 100 million degrees Celsius or more, until it is a plasma, a gas of bare nuclei and loose electrons. Why does fusion need such enormous heat?
questions.answer: Only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away
choices: Only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away
Only very hot nuclei melt enough to flow into one another
Only great heat can break the nuclei into loose protons first
Only very hot fuel can burn with oxygen into helium
questions.context: Every nucleus carries a positive charge, so two nuclei push each other away, and only nuclei moving very fast, which means very hot, come close enough for the short-range strong force to take hold. When deuterium and tritium fuse, the helium and spare neutron that come out have a little less mass than the fuel that went in, and the missing mass leaves as energy; nothing burns. Machines hold the hot plasma in strong magnetic fields, as in a tokamak, or crush tiny fuel pellets with lasers.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches fusion as light nuclei joining, and the repulsion that only great heat overcomes is why fusion is so hard on Earth.

questions.question: Scientists at the National Ignition Facility in California aimed 192 lasers at a tiny frozen pellet of deuterium and tritium, two heavy kinds of hydrogen, on 5 December 2022. The pellet's nuclei fused, and the team announced that for the first time a shot had reached ignition, a goal fusion scientists had chased for decades. What did ignition mean?
questions.answer: The pellet gave out more energy than the lasers put in
choices: The pellet gave out more energy than the lasers put in
The laboratory made more energy than it drew from the grid
The fusion energy was sent out as electricity to homes
The pellet went on fusing by itself for hours afterwards
questions.context: The fusion gave out 3.15 megajoules against the 2.05 megajoules of laser light fired into the tiny gold can that held the pellet, the first time any fusion experiment had got more energy out of its fuel than its lasers put in. But the lasers drew about 300 megajoules from the grid for that split-second shot, and no fusion machine yet makes more electricity than it uses, so whether fusion can power cities is still an open question. Later shots there have given out more than 8 megajoules.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders study fusion power research, and what the 2022 ignition did and did not show is the honest state of that research.

questions.question: Nuclear power plants make about a tenth of the world's electricity. A plant runs day and night whatever the weather, and over its whole life it gives off about as little carbon dioxide for each unit of electricity as a wind farm does. Every year or two, though, part of its fuel is used up and comes out of the reactor. What makes that used fuel hard to store?
questions.answer: It stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years
choices: It stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years
It is a liquid that can easily leak out of its tanks
It piles up by the millions of tonnes every year
It escapes from its casks whenever it is moved by road or rail
questions.context: Used fuel is solid ceramic pellets sealed in metal rods; it cools for years in pools of water, which carry off its heat and block its radiation, and then goes into sealed casks of steel and concrete. All the used fuel American power plants have made since the 1950s would fit on one football field less than 10 yards deep, and thousands of cask shipments have crossed the country without any radioactive material escaping. It must be kept away from people for thousands of years: Finland has built the world's first deep underground store for it, but the United States still has no permanent store, its plan for one at Yucca Mountain halted since 2010.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science weighs nuclear power's benefits against its risks, and long-lived radioactive waste is the main one.

cbe156dffb.why: Fact-check (error): the card said the strong force 'never reaches the electrons' because of its short reach; range is not the reason, since electrons do not feel the strong force at all (they carry no colour charge, F28). The card now says so in the fact-check's words. Judge (medium, tell): the stem's 'packed side by side' and 'at such close quarters' echoed the key 'right beside it'; the stem now says 'packed tightly together' and 'at that tiny distance', and the key is 'To the particles right next to it' (not the judge's 'nearest neighbours', which could be read as the neighbouring atoms of the third choice, and not 'protons and neutrons', which would echo the stem's last line).

06b6b0598d.why: Fact-check (uncertain): 'nearly thirty years' undershot a partnership that ran from late 1907 to July 1938; the stem now says 'some thirty years' (F29). Fact-check (optional nuance): the card no longer says they held back 'as chemists', since their paper said that as chemists they had to name barium and as nuclear chemists they hesitated; it now says only that they held back from explaining it (F8). Key and choices unchanged.

7c6e1c0235.why: Judge (low, safety lane): 'in a lump of such uranium ... the splitting spreads through the lump' pictured a growing chain in a lump of pure uranium-235, the bomb picture. The chain is now set in a reactor's fuel, one split setting off the next, in the judge's words. No design, enrichment or critical-mass detail anywhere. Key, choices and card unchanged.

eff142c470.why: Fact-check (error): 'the same water carries the heat away as steam' is false for pressurised water reactors, more than 65% of US reactors, where the core water is kept from boiling and heats a separate loop that becomes the steam (F30). The card now says the water 'carries the heat away to make the steam', true of both kinds. Stem, key and choices unchanged.

994f30454a.why: Fact-check (error): the laser light did not reach the pellet; it went into the gold hohlraum, which turned it to X-rays that crushed the capsule, and the capsule itself took in only about 250 kJ (F31). The card now says the light was 'fired into the tiny gold can that held the pellet'. Stem, key and choices unchanged.

928d5d3fa3.why: Fact-check (error): 'no release of radiation' taught that casks let none out, when DOE's claim is that no radioactive material escaped; the card now says 'without any radioactive material escaping'. Fact-check (note): the lure 'It leaks radiation whenever it is moved' could be defended, since a loaded cask always gives off a little radiation through its walls; it now reads 'It escapes from its casks whenever it is moved by road or rail', wrong on DOE's record (F26). Judge (low, stance): the card answered every lure with reassurance and gave the hazard one clause; it now states the open problem as flatly as the benefits, that the United States has no permanent store and its Yucca Mountain plan has been halted since 2010 (F27, F32). Stem and key unchanged.
